quote: A one-dimensional potential $p^2+V(x)$ has, at each energy, exactly one periodic orbit: the back-and-forth motion between the two turning points.
problem: Stated for any one-dimensional potential, but it holds only for a single-well confining potential, where $V(x)=E$ has exactly two solutions. Counterexample: the double well $V=(x^2-1)^2$ at $E=0.5$ (below the barrier height $V(0)=1$) has four turning points and two disjoint periodic orbits, one in each well. The hypothesis matters here because the paper's fitted potentials $V+\delta V$ carry large wiggles (max $|\delta V|=199$ where $V\approx500$, Sec. III) and need not be monotone on each side. The same unqualified claim recurs in the Key Ideas ('a 1D potential has one orbit per energy').
fix: A one-dimensional single-well potential $p^2+V(x)$ (one for which $V(x)=E$ has exactly two solutions, such as the smooth Wu--Sprung potential) has, at each energy, exactly one periodic orbit: the back-and-forth motion between the two turning points. A potential with several wells can have several such orbits at one energy, one per well, but still only finitely many, each confined between neighboring turning points.
